Only women employed by the State Government
Only students below 18 years with school identity cards
All residents of neighbouring States on private buses

The benefit is not restricted to government employees.
The stated beneficiaries are not limited to school students.

Only public-sector undertakings
Only registered agricultural cooperatives
Scheduled Caste, Scheduled Tribe and persons-with-disabilities entrepreneurs

questions.topic: Logical Reasoning; Analytical Ability and Data Interpretation
questions.stem: A storage tank is 60% full. After 120 litres are added, it becomes 80% full. What is the tank's total capacity?
options: 400 litres
500 litres
600 litres
800 litres
explanations: A 400-litre tank would gain only 80 litres between 60% and 80%.
A 500-litre tank would gain 100 litres over that interval.
Correct. The 20-percentage-point increase equals 120 litres, so capacity = 120/0.20 = 600 litres.
An 800-litre tank would require 160 litres for a 20-point increase.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: Logical Reasoning; Analytical Ability and Data Interpretation; source/basis: Standard quantitative aptitude: percentages and proportional reasoning; R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude

questions.topic: Logical Reasoning; Analytical Ability and Data Interpretation
questions.stem: Statements: All filtration units are treatment components. No treatment component is disposable. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: No filtration unit is disposable
Some filtration units are disposable
Every non-disposable object is a filtration unit
No treatment component is a filtration unit
explanations: Correct. Every filtration unit belongs to the treatment-component class, and that class has no disposable members.
This directly contradicts the second statement when applied to filtration units.
The premises do not say that all non-disposable objects are filtration units.
The first statement says filtration units are treatment components, not that the two classes are disjoint.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: Logical Reasoning; Analytical Ability and Data Interpretation; source/basis: Standard verbal reasoning: categorical syllogisms; R.S. Aggarwal, A Modern Approach to Verbal & Non-Verbal Reasoning

questions.stem: Choose the grammatically correct completion: “No sooner had the pump started ___ the pressure indicator began to fluctuate.”
options: when
then
as
than
explanations: 'No sooner' is conventionally paired with 'than', not 'when'.
'Then' does not complete the standard correlative construction.
'As' is not the required conjunction in this pattern.
Correct. The standard construction is 'No sooner ... than ...', with subject–auxiliary inversion after 'No sooner'.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: Basic English (10th class Standard); source/basis: Wren & Martin, High School English Grammar and Composition, correlative conjunctions and inversion

questions.stem: In the sentence “The engineer adopted a prudent maintenance schedule,” the word 'prudent' most nearly means:
options: Reckless
Careful and sensible
Unavoidable
Expensive
explanations: Reckless is nearly the opposite of prudent.
Correct. Prudent means showing care, good judgement and foresight.
Unavoidable describes necessity, not judgement.
Expensive refers to cost and is not the meaning of prudent.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: Basic English (10th class Standard); source/basis: Oxford Learner's Dictionaries, prudent; standard competitive-exam vocabulary

questions.stem: Choose the correct reported form of: The engineer said, “I am inspecting the valve now.”
options: The engineer said that I am inspecting the valve now.
The engineer said that he is inspecting the valve tomorrow.
The engineer said that he was inspecting the valve then.
The engineer said that he had inspected the valve yesterday.
explanations: The pronoun does not normally remain 'I' when reporting the engineer's statement in the third person.
The tense and time expression have not been adjusted for ordinary indirect speech.
Correct. Present progressive commonly backshifts to past progressive and 'now' changes to 'then' in this reported context.
This changes the action to past perfect and 'yesterday', which the original statement did not say.
questions.basis: Official Paper I syllabus: Basic English (10th class Standard); source/basis: Wren & Martin, High School English Grammar and Composition, direct and indirect speech

questions.stem: A call centre receives calls according to a Poisson process with mean 2 calls per minute. What is the probability of receiving exactly two calls in a one-minute interval? (Use e^-2 ≈ 0.1353.)
explanations: 0.1353 is P(X=0) for λ=2, not P(X=2).
0.4060 is not obtained from the Poisson probability mass function at k=2.
0.5413 exceeds the exact probability and is not the calculated value.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Probability and Statistics; source/basis: Sheldon Ross, A First Course in Probability, Poisson distribution and probability mass function

questions.stem: A random variable X is uniformly distributed over the interval [2,8]. What is Var(X)?
explanations: Correct. For U(a,b), variance is (b−a)²/12 = 6²/12 = 3.
6 is the interval width, not the variance.
9 is the squared half-width, not the variance.
12 does not follow from the uniform-variance formula.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Probability and Statistics; source/basis: Devore, Probability and Statistics for Engineering and the Sciences, continuous uniform distribution

questions.stem: Suppose X is normally distributed with mean 70 and standard deviation 10. Approximately what is P(X > 85)?
explanations: 0.9332 is approximately P(X<85), the complementary tail.
0.5 is the probability above the mean 70, not above 85.
0.1587 is the upper-tail probability beyond z=1, not z=1.5.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Probability and Statistics; source/basis: Standard normal distribution table; Devore, Probability and Statistics for Engineering and the Sciences

questions.stem: A random variable X has variance 4. If Y=3X+5, what is Var(Y)?
explanations: 12 is 3·Var(X), but variance scales by the square of the multiplier.
17 incorrectly adds the constant 5 to a variance.
Correct. Var(aX+b)=a²Var(X), so Var(Y)=3²×4=36.
41 incorrectly adds both the scale and constant rather than applying the variance rule.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Probability and Statistics; source/basis: Casella and Berger, Statistical Inference, expectation and variance under transformations

questions.stem: Which statement is the Cayley–Hamilton theorem for a square matrix A?
options: A is always equal to its transpose
Every eigenvalue of A is zero
A commutes with every matrix of the same order
A satisfies its own characteristic polynomial
explanations: The theorem does not assert that A is symmetric.
It does not force all eigenvalues to be zero.
Commutativity with every same-order matrix is false in general.
Correct. If p(λ)=det(λI−A) is the characteristic polynomial, then p(A)=0.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Set Theory & Algebra; Linear Algebra; source/basis: Lay, Linear Algebra and Its Applications; standard Cayley–Hamilton theorem

questions.subtopic: Generators of a finite cyclic group
questions.stem: How many generators does a cyclic group of order 18 have?
explanations: Correct. A cyclic group of order n has φ(n) generators; φ(18)=18(1−1/2)(1−1/3)=6.
9 elements are not generators of a cyclic group of order 18.
A cyclic group of order 18 has 18 elements but only six generators.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Set Theory & Algebra; Linear Algebra; source/basis: Gallian, Contemporary Abstract Algebra, cyclic groups and Euler's totient function

questions.stem: What is the multiplicative inverse of 12 modulo 35?
explanations: 12×2=24, which is not congruent to 1 modulo 35.
Correct. 12×3=36≡1 (mod 35), so 3 is the inverse.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Set Theory & Algebra; Linear Algebra; source/basis: Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, modular arithmetic and inverses

questions.stem: For a group homomorphism φ:G→H, which property must the kernel ker(φ) have?
options: It is a normal subgroup of G
It must equal G in every homomorphism
It must contain every element of H
It must be a cyclic subgroup of prime order
explanations: Correct. The kernel is a subgroup and is normal because gkg⁻¹ maps to the identity for every g∈G and k∈ker(φ).
The kernel equals G only for the trivial homomorphism, not every homomorphism.
The kernel is a subset of G, not H.
A kernel need not be cyclic or have prime order.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Set Theory & Algebra; Linear Algebra; source/basis: Gallian, Contemporary Abstract Algebra, kernels and normal subgroups

questions.topic: Combinatorics and Discrete Structures; Graph Theory; Mathematical Logic
questions.stem: Let a₀=1 and aₙ=3aₙ₋₁+2 for n≥1. Which closed form satisfies this recurrence?
explanations: For n=0 this gives 2, not the required a₀=1.
Correct. At n=0 it gives 1; substituting gives 3(2·3ⁿ⁻¹−1)+2=2·3ⁿ−1.
At n=0 this gives 4, not 1, and it does not satisfy the recurrence.
At n=0 this gives −1, not 1.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Combinatorics and Discrete Structures; Graph Theory; Mathematical Logic; source/basis: Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, recurrence relations

questions.topic: Combinatorics and Discrete Structures; Graph Theory; Mathematical Logic
questions.stem: Three sets A, B and C have sizes 40, 35 and 30. Their pairwise intersections have sizes 10, 8 and 6, and |A∩B∩C|=3. What is |A∪B∪C|?
explanations: 78 omits the required correction for the triple intersection.
81 is the sum of individual sizes minus pairwise intersections, without adding the triple intersection back.
90 is the sum of the three set sizes and ignores all overlaps.

questions.topic: Combinatorics and Discrete Structures; Graph Theory; Mathematical Logic
questions.stem: A connected undirected graph has exactly two vertices of odd degree. Which statement is necessarily true?
options: It has an Euler circuit but no Euler trail
It has neither an Euler trail nor an Euler circuit
It has an Euler trail using every edge exactly once, but no Euler circuit
It must be a tree
explanations: An Euler circuit requires every vertex to have even degree.
A connected graph with two odd-degree vertices does have an Euler trail.
Correct. A connected graph has an Euler trail exactly when it has zero or two odd-degree vertices; with two, it has no Euler circuit.
The degree condition does not imply that the graph is acyclic or a tree.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Combinatorics and Discrete Structures; Graph Theory; Mathematical Logic; source/basis: Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, Euler trails and circuits

questions.subtopic: Counting binary strings with no consecutive ones
questions.stem: How many binary strings of length 6 contain no two consecutive 1s?
explanations: 13 is too small; the count follows the Fibonacci recurrence with initial values 1,2.
18 is not the Fibonacci count for length 6.
Correct. If f(n) counts such strings, f(n)=f(n−1)+f(n−2), f(1)=2 and f(2)=3; hence f(6)=21.
32 counts all binary strings without restricting adjacent 1s.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Combinatorics and Discrete Structures; Graph Theory; Mathematical Logic; source/basis: Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, recurrence counting

questions.stem: For a cross-coupled NOR SR latch with active-high S and R inputs, which input combination is the forbidden or invalid condition?
explanations: Correct. With both NOR inputs asserted, both outputs are driven low, violating the complementary-state requirement; release can lead to an indeterminate state.
S=1, R=0 is the set condition for the conventional NOR latch.
S=0, R=1 is the reset condition.
S=0, R=0 is the hold condition for a NOR SR latch.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Digital Logic; source/basis: Mano and Ciletti, Digital Design, SR latch truth table

questions.stem: In a two-level sum-of-products circuit, two adjacent input combinations both produce output 1, but the corresponding minterms are covered by separate product terms with no common implicant. Which correction most directly removes the resulting static-1 hazard?
options: Delete one of the product terms
Add a redundant consensus/bridging product term that covers the adjacent transition
Invert the output permanently
Replace every AND gate with an OR gate
explanations: Deleting a required product term may change the Boolean function rather than remove only the hazard.
Correct. A redundant consensus term provides overlapping coverage during the input transition and removes the static-1 hazard.
Inverting the output changes the function and does not solve the hazard as stated.
Replacing gate types indiscriminately changes the implemented logic.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Digital Logic; source/basis: Mano and Ciletti, Digital Design, hazards in combinational circuits

questions.subtopic: Implementing a Boolean function with a 4-to-1 multiplexer
questions.stem: A 4-to-1 multiplexer uses A and B as its select inputs to implement F(A,B,C)=Σm(1,2,6,7), with A as the most significant variable. Which data-input assignment (D0,D1,D2,D3) is correct for select codes AB=00,01,10,11?
explanations: Correct. For AB=00, F=C; for 01, F=C′; for 10, F=0; for 11, F=1.
This reverses the first two cofactors and the last two constants.
This assigns the cofactors to the wrong select combinations.
This also assigns the cofactors and constants to the wrong select codes.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Digital Logic; source/basis: Mano and Ciletti, Digital Design, Shannon expansion and multiplexer implementation

questions.stem: After adding two valid BCD digits, when must a BCD adder add 0110₂ to the four-bit sum?
options: Whenever the binary sum is odd
Only when the lower digit is zero
When the four-bit sum exceeds 1001₂ or a carry out occurs
Whenever the sum is less than 1001₂
explanations: Oddness of the sum is unrelated to BCD correction.
A zero lower digit is not the correction condition.
Correct. A binary sum above 9 is not a valid BCD digit; adding six corrects the digit, including the carry-out case.
A sum below or equal to 9 is already a valid BCD digit and needs no correction.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Digital Logic; source/basis: Mano and Ciletti, Digital Design, BCD addition

questions.stem: A direct-mapped cache contains 64 lines. Main-memory block number 130 is referenced. Using zero-based line numbering, which cache line is selected?
explanations: 130 mod 64 is not 0.
Correct. The line index is block number modulo number of lines: 130 mod 64=2.
4 is not the remainder of 130 divided by 64.
6 is not the remainder of 130 divided by 64.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Organization and Architecture; source/basis: Patterson and Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design, direct-mapped cache indexing

questions.stem: In cycle-stealing Direct Memory Access (DMA), what does the DMA controller do?
options: It takes individual memory/bus cycles for transfers, temporarily delaying the CPU's use of the bus
It permanently disables the CPU while a device transfers data
It copies every byte through a CPU register and is therefore programmed I/O
It changes the virtual address space of the process
explanations: Correct. Cycle stealing interleaves DMA transfers with CPU activity by taking selected bus cycles.
The CPU is not permanently disabled; this describes an extreme burst-transfer misconception.
DMA is specifically intended to avoid requiring the CPU to move each byte through its registers.
DMA does not alter a process's virtual address space.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Organization and Architecture; source/basis: Stallings, Computer Organization and Architecture, DMA transfer modes

questions.stem: A five-stage instruction pipeline executes 20 instructions with no stalls, no fill/drain overhead beyond the stages, and one instruction entering each cycle. How many clock cycles are required to complete all instructions?
explanations: 20 cycles would ignore the initial pipeline fill.
23 omits one of the five stages in the fill-plus-throughput calculation.
Correct. Ideal cycles = k+n−1 = 5+20−1 = 24.
100 cycles is the unpipelined total for five stages per instruction.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Organization and Architecture; source/basis: Patterson and Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design, pipeline latency and throughput

questions.stem: In C, let `int a[6] = {4, 7, 9, 12, 15, 18}; int *p = a;`. What value is produced by `*(p + 3)`?
explanations: p points to a[0], so this is not the first element.
p+2 would point to a[2], whose value is 9.
Correct. Pointer addition is scaled by the pointed-to type; p+3 points to a[3], whose value is 12.
p+4 points to a[4], whose value is 15.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Programming and Data Structures; source/basis: ISO C11 draft N1570, pointer arithmetic and array subscripting, §§6.5.2.1 and 6.5.6

questions.subtopic: Circular queue full condition with one reserved slot
questions.stem: A circular queue of array capacity N uses the convention that one slot is always left unused to distinguish full from empty. With `front` pointing to the first element and `rear` to the next insertion position, which condition indicates that the queue is full?
options: front == rear
(rear + 1) % N == front
rear == N
front == 0
explanations: Under this representation, front==rear denotes the empty queue.
Correct. Advancing rear by one modulo N would collide with front, so the reserved-slot queue is full.
rear may wrap around and need not equal N.
front being zero says nothing by itself about fullness.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Programming and Data Structures; source/basis: Mark Allen Weiss, Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis, circular-array queue implementation

questions.stem: In Floyd's tortoise-and-hare algorithm for detecting a cycle in a singly linked list, how are the two pointers advanced during each iteration?
options: Both pointers advance by one node
The slow pointer advances by two nodes and the fast pointer by one
The slow pointer advances by one node and the fast pointer by two
The fast pointer moves to the last node on every iteration
explanations: If both move at the same speed, the method cannot force a catch-up within a cycle.
The speeds are reversed in this option.
Correct. The fast pointer gains one node per iteration relative to the slow pointer and eventually meets it if a cycle exists.
The fast pointer follows links; it does not jump directly to the last node.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Programming and Data Structures; source/basis: Weiss, Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis, linked-list cycle detection

questions.stem: Counting sort is applied to n integer keys known to lie in the range 0 through k. What is its standard time complexity?
options: Θ(n log n)
Θ(n+k)
Θ(k log n)
Θ(n²)
explanations: Counting sort is not comparison-based and does not require n log n comparisons.
Correct. Counting the key frequencies, forming cumulative counts and placing the n items takes Θ(n+k) time.
There is no k log n sorting step in the standard algorithm.
Quadratic time is not the standard counting-sort bound.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Algorithms; source/basis: CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, 4th ed., counting sort

questions.stem: Which statement about the Bellman–Ford single-source shortest-path algorithm is correct?
options: It requires all edge weights to be non-negative
It works only on undirected acyclic graphs
It cannot detect negative-weight cycles
It supports negative edge weights and can detect a reachable negative-weight cycle
explanations: The non-negative-weight restriction is associated with Dijkstra's algorithm, not Bellman–Ford.
Bellman–Ford applies to directed graphs and does not require acyclicity.
An additional relaxation pass can reveal a reachable negative-weight cycle.
Correct. Bellman–Ford relaxes edges repeatedly and reports a reachable negative cycle if further relaxation remains possible.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Algorithms; source/basis: CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, 4th ed., Bellman–Ford algorithm

questions.stem: In A* search for a shortest path, a heuristic h(n) is admissible when it:
options: Never overestimates the true minimum remaining cost to a goal
Always equals the exact remaining cost
Is greater than the true remaining cost at every non-goal node
Depends only on the number of edges already traversed
explanations: Correct. An admissible heuristic is optimistic: h(n)≤h*(n) for every node.
Equality is sufficient but not required; an admissible heuristic may underestimate.
Overestimation violates admissibility and can destroy the optimality guarantee.
The heuristic estimates remaining cost, not merely the path already travelled.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Algorithms; source/basis: Russell and Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, A* search and admissible heuristics

questions.subtopic: Closure of deterministic context-free languages under complement
questions.stem: Which closure property is guaranteed for deterministic context-free languages (DCFLs)?
options: Closure under arbitrary intersection of two DCFLs
Closure under complement
Closure under arbitrary union of two DCFLs
Closure under reversal in every case
explanations: DCFLs are not closed under arbitrary intersection.
Correct. A deterministic pushdown automaton can be complemented by exchanging accepting and rejecting outcomes after ensuring the machine halts appropriately.
DCFLs are not closed under arbitrary union.
Reversal is not a general closure property of DCFLs.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Theory of Computation; source/basis: Hopcroft, Motwani and Ullman, Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation, deterministic context-free languages

questions.stem: Rice's theorem states that which class of properties of Turing-machine-recognisable languages is undecidable?
options: Every syntactic property of a machine's state names
Only properties concerning the number of tape symbols
Every non-trivial semantic property of the language/function recognised or computed
Only properties of finite automata
explanations: Renaming states is a syntactic change and is not the subject of Rice's theorem.
The theorem is not restricted to tape-alphabet size.
Correct. Any non-trivial property depending on the language/function recognised by a Turing machine is undecidable in general.
Rice's theorem concerns Turing-computable behaviour, not only finite automata.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Theory of Computation; source/basis: Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed., Rice's theorem

questions.subtopic: Linear bounded automata and context-sensitive languages
questions.stem: Which computational model characterises the class of context-sensitive languages?
options: Finite automata
Pushdown automata with one stack
Unrestricted Turing machines with no space bound
Linear bounded automata
explanations: Finite automata recognise regular languages.
Pushdown automata characterise context-free languages.
Unrestricted Turing machines recognise recursively enumerable languages.
Correct. Context-sensitive languages are exactly those recognised by linear bounded automata.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Theory of Computation; source/basis: Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed., context-sensitive languages

questions.stem: A context-free grammar is ambiguous if there exists at least one string in its language that:
options: Has two distinct parse trees (equivalently, two distinct leftmost derivations)
Cannot be generated by any derivation
Contains no terminal symbols
Has exactly one derivation of every possible type
explanations: Correct. Ambiguity requires at least one string with more than one distinct parse tree or leftmost derivation.
A string generated by the grammar is not un-generable.
A string may contain terminals; ambiguity is about its structural derivations.
Ambiguity is the existence of multiple parse structures, not uniqueness.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Theory of Computation; source/basis: Hopcroft, Motwani and Ullman, Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation, CFG ambiguity

questions.stem: For a grammar production A→Aα | β, where β does not begin with A, which standard transformation removes this direct left recursion?
options: A→Aβ; β→α
A→βA′; A′→αA′ | ε
A→αβ; A′→ε
A→β; A′→Aα
explanations: This retains direct left recursion in A.
Correct. The transformed grammar first derives β and then repeats α through A′, with ε allowing termination.
This does not preserve the original language in general.
This does not express the repeated α suffix correctly.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Compiler Design; source/basis: Aho, Lam, Sethi and Ullman, Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools, 2nd ed., left-recursion elimination

questions.stem: During construction of an LL(1) predictive parsing table, two different productions for the same nonterminal are entered in the same table cell M[A,a]. What does this indicate?
options: The grammar is necessarily regular
The grammar has no ε-productions
The grammar is not LL(1) as written because the parser cannot choose a unique production using one lookahead symbol
The grammar is automatically unambiguous
explanations: A parsing-table conflict does not imply regularity.
A conflict can occur with or without ε-productions.
Correct. An LL(1) parser must have at most one production in each table entry for a nonterminal and lookahead terminal.
A table conflict does not prove that the grammar is unambiguous.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Compiler Design; source/basis: Aho, Lam, Sethi and Ullman, Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools, 2nd ed., LL(1) parsing tables

questions.stem: In an attribute grammar, a synthesized attribute of a parse-tree node is normally computed from:
options: Attributes of its parent only
The lexical order of all tokens in the source file
The node's future siblings only
Attributes of the node's children and local information
explanations: Attributes passed from a parent to a child are inherited attributes, not synthesized ones.
Token order alone is not the defining rule for a synthesized attribute.
A synthesized attribute is computed bottom-up from the node's descendants, not from future siblings.
Correct. Synthesized attributes flow from child nodes towards their parent in the parse tree.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Compiler Design; source/basis: Aho, Lam, Sethi and Ullman, Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools, syntax-directed definitions

questions.stem: In the Banker's deadlock-avoidance algorithm, a state is safe when:
options: At least one process has a zero maximum resource claim
A sequence exists in which every process can obtain its remaining need, finish, and release its allocation
No process currently holds any resource
The total number of resources is greater than the number of processes
explanations: A zero maximum claim is not required for safety.
Correct. A safe sequence demonstrates that all processes can finish in some order using currently available resources plus resources released by completed processes.
Processes may hold resources in a safe state.
A numerical comparison between total resources and process count is not the safety criterion.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Operating Systems; source/basis: Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts, deadlock avoidance

questions.subtopic: LRU stack property and Belady's anomaly
questions.stem: Which statement about the Least Recently Used (LRU) page-replacement algorithm is correct?
options: LRU is a stack algorithm and therefore does not exhibit Belady's anomaly
LRU always produces more page faults than FIFO
LRU requires the reference string to be sorted by page number
LRU replaces the page with the largest virtual address
explanations: Correct. LRU has the stack/inclusion property: increasing the number of frames cannot increase its page-fault count.
There is no universal rule that LRU produces more faults than FIFO.
Page references are processed in their temporal order, not sorted by page number.
Replacement is based on recency of use, not virtual-address magnitude.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Operating Systems; source/basis: Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts, LRU and stack algorithms

questions.stem: How does LOOK disk scheduling differ from SCAN?
options: LOOK always moves to cylinder zero before reversing
LOOK reverses direction only after a fixed time quantum
LOOK reverses at the last pending request in the current direction instead of travelling to the physical end of the disk
LOOK serves requests in random order
explanations: LOOK need not travel to cylinder zero unless it is the last request in that direction.
A time quantum is not the LOOK reversal rule.
Correct. LOOK 'looks' for the final request in the current direction and reverses there, avoiding unnecessary travel to the disk boundary.
Random service describes neither LOOK nor SCAN.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Operating Systems; source/basis: Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts, disk scheduling

questions.stem: What does `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC)` produce in a SQL query?
options: One aggregated row per department
A unique sequential row number within each department partition, ordered by descending salary
A count of all employees with the same salary
A ranking that always assigns equal numbers to tied salaries
explanations: The window function does not collapse rows into one aggregate row per department.
Correct. ROW_NUMBER assigns 1, 2, 3, ... separately within each department partition according to the specified ordering.
It does not count employees by salary.
Tied sort values still receive distinct row numbers; RANK or DENSE_RANK behave differently.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Databases; source/basis: PostgreSQL documentation, window functions; Elmasri and Navathe, Fundamentals of Database Systems

questions.stem: What is the principal concurrency benefit of multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) in a transactional database?
options: It eliminates the need for transaction isolation
It stores only one physical version of every row
It forces every reader to acquire an exclusive lock on every row
It can let readers use a consistent snapshot while writers create newer row versions
explanations: MVCC does not eliminate isolation semantics; it is one way to implement them.
Multiple versions, rather than only one, are central to MVCC.
Readers generally do not need exclusive locks merely to read an MVCC snapshot.
Correct. Versioned reads can avoid many read-write blocking conflicts while preserving a transactionally consistent snapshot.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Databases; source/basis: PostgreSQL documentation, MVCC introduction; Elmasri and Navathe, Fundamentals of Database Systems

questions.stem: A control-flow graph has E=10 edges, N=8 nodes and one connected component (P=1). What is its cyclomatic complexity?
explanations: E−N+2P is not 2 for these values.
The result is not 3 when the component term is included.
Correct. V(G)=E−N+2P=10−8+2=4.
5 would require one additional edge or a different graph count.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Information Systems and Software Engineering; source/basis: McCabe, A Complexity Measure; Pressman and Maxim, Software Engineering, cyclomatic complexity

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of mutation testing in software quality assurance?
options: To measure execution speed under maximum load
To assess whether a test suite detects small, deliberately introduced faults in the program
To automatically convert source code from one language to another
To prove that the program contains no defects
explanations: Performance benchmarking is a different testing activity.
Correct. Mutants are small program changes; tests that detect them provide evidence about the fault-detection strength of the test suite.
Language translation is not the purpose of mutation testing.
No practical test technique proves the complete absence of all defects.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Information Systems and Software Engineering; source/basis: ISTQB Foundation Level syllabus, test techniques; Pressman and Maxim, Software Engineering

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes software verification from software validation?
options: Verification checks conformance to specified requirements; validation checks whether the resulting system meets user needs
Verification is performed only after deployment; validation only before coding
Verification and validation are identical terms
Validation checks coding style, while verification checks market demand
explanations: Correct. Verification asks whether the product is being built according to specification; validation asks whether the right product is being built for users.
Both activities can occur throughout development; they are not restricted to those single phases.
They are related but distinct quality activities.
The definitions are reversed and do not capture the standard distinction.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Information Systems and Software Engineering; source/basis: ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 software life-cycle processes; Pressman and Maxim, Software Engineering

questions.stem: In TCP, which mechanism primarily communicates how much additional data the receiver is currently prepared to accept?
options: The sender's congestion window (cwnd)
The IP time-to-live field
The DNS resource-record TTL
The receiver-advertised window (rwnd)
explanations: The congestion window reflects the sender's estimate of network capacity, not the receiver's buffer advertisement.
IP TTL limits packet lifetime/hop count.
DNS TTL controls caching duration for resource records.
Correct. The advertised receive window communicates receiver-side flow-control capacity.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Networks; source/basis: Kurose and Ross, Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach; RFC 9293, Transmission Control Protocol

questions.subtopic: IPv6 multicast and absence of broadcast
questions.stem: Which statement about IPv6 delivery semantics is correct?
options: IPv6 uses broadcast addresses in the same way as IPv4
IPv6 has no broadcast; multicast is used for one-to-many delivery and functions such as neighbour discovery
IPv6 forbids multicast
IPv6 replaces all unicast addressing with anycast
explanations: IPv6 does not define broadcast addressing as IPv4 does.
Correct. IPv6 uses multicast for group delivery and neighbour-discovery functions.
Multicast is a fundamental part of IPv6.
IPv6 continues to support unicast and multicast; anycast is an additional addressing mode.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Networks; source/basis: RFC 8200, Internet Protocol, Version 6 (IPv6) Specification; RFC 4861, Neighbor Discovery

questions.stem: An IPv6 router cannot forward a packet because it is larger than the next-link MTU. What is the normal IPv6 behaviour?
options: The router fragments the packet into smaller fragments
The router silently discards it and never informs the source
The router discards it and sends an ICMPv6 Packet Too Big message so the source can adjust packet size
The router converts the packet into an IPv4 datagram
explanations: IPv6 routers do not fragment packets in transit.
Silently discarding without the required feedback would prevent proper Path MTU Discovery.
Correct. The router sends ICMPv6 Packet Too Big; the source adapts the packet size or performs source fragmentation where appropriate.
IPv6 forwarding does not translate a packet into IPv4.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Computer Networks; source/basis: RFC 8201, Path MTU Discovery for IP version 6; RFC 4443, ICMPv6

questions.stem: In XML, what is the principal role of a namespace name such as `urn:example:inventory`?
options: It uniquely identifies an element/attribute vocabulary; it need not be a retrievable web page
It specifies the physical directory in which the XML file must be stored
It encrypts all elements using the named protocol
It determines the order in which XML elements are parsed
explanations: Correct. A namespace URI is an identifier used to distinguish names; XML processors do not have to retrieve it as a document.
A namespace name does not prescribe file-system storage.
Namespaces do not provide encryption.
Parsing order follows XML structure and grammar, not the namespace identifier.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Web Technologies; source/basis: W3C, Namespaces in XML 1.0 Recommendation: https://www.w3.org/TR/xml-names/

questions.stem: In a JSP page, what is the type and purpose of the implicit object `out`?
options: A JDBC Connection used for database queries
A JspWriter used to write response content
A ServletContext used to access application-wide attributes
An HttpSession used to retain user-specific state
explanations: Database connections are not represented by the JSP `out` object.
Correct. `out` is the JspWriter associated with the response output stream.
The application-wide context is exposed through the `application` implicit object.
User-session state is exposed through `session`.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Web Technologies; source/basis: Jakarta Server Pages specification, implicit objects; Oracle Java EE JSP tutorial

questions.stem: In PHP, which superglobal array normally contains form fields submitted in the body of an HTTP POST request using the standard form encoding?
options: $_GET
$_SERVER
$_POST
$_COOKIE
explanations: $_GET contains query-string parameters.
$_SERVER contains server and request environment information.
Correct. $_POST contains form variables submitted using POST form encoding.
$_COOKIE contains cookie values sent by the browser.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Web Technologies; source/basis: PHP Manual, Variables From External Sources: https://www.php.net/manual/en/reserved.variables.post.php

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the HTTP response directives `Cache-Control: no-store` and `Cache-Control: no-cache`?
options: Both require every response to be encrypted
no-store allows storage but requires revalidation; no-cache forbids storage
no-store forbids caches from storing the response; no-cache permits storage but requires revalidation before reuse
no-store applies only to cookies, while no-cache applies only to HTML
explanations: Neither directive is an encryption mechanism.
The meanings are reversed in this option.
Correct. `no-store` prohibits storage; `no-cache` allows storage but requires successful validation before reuse.
The directives apply to HTTP caching generally, not only cookies or HTML.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Web Technologies; source/basis: RFC 9111, HTTP Caching, Cache-Control directives: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111

questions.subtopic: HTML async versus defer script loading
questions.stem: For a classic external script in HTML, which statement about the `defer` attribute is correct?
options: The script is downloaded in parallel and executed after document parsing, in document order
The script blocks parsing while it downloads and executes immediately
The script executes before the HTML parser reaches the script element
The script is executed only after the user clicks the page
explanations: Correct. Deferred classic scripts execute after parsing completes and preserve document order relative to other deferred classic scripts.
This describes a parser-blocking script without async/defer.
Execution before the parser reaches the element is not the defer behaviour.
The attribute does not make execution depend on a user click.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Web Technologies; source/basis: WHATWG HTML Living Standard, script processing model: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html

questions.topic: OOPS Concepts, Programming in C++ and JAVA
questions.stem: In Java, a subclass declares a static method with the same signature as a static method in its superclass. How is the selected method normally determined?
options: By runtime overriding based on the object's dynamic class
By the reference/expression type at compile time; static methods are hidden, not overridden polymorphically
By the most recently loaded class file
By the value of the method's return object
explanations: Runtime overriding applies to instance methods, not static method dispatch.
Correct. Static method selection is based on the compile-time type of the qualifying reference or class name.
Class-loading order does not define static method selection.
A returned object's value does not determine which static method is invoked.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: OOPS Concepts, Programming in C++ and JAVA; source/basis: Java Language Specification, §8.4.8.2, Hiding (by Class Methods)

questions.topic: OOPS Concepts, Programming in C++ and JAVA
questions.subtopic: C++ virtual inheritance in diamond hierarchy
questions.stem: In a C++ diamond-shaped inheritance hierarchy, both intermediate classes inherit from the same base class. What is the purpose of declaring that base inheritance as `virtual`?
options: To make all base-class functions pure virtual
To prevent construction of any derived object
To force every method call to use static binding
To ensure the most-derived object contains one shared base-class subobject rather than duplicate base subobjects
explanations: Virtual inheritance does not make all base functions pure virtual.
It does not prohibit constructing the derived object.
It does not control static versus dynamic method binding.
Correct. Virtual base classes ensure a single shared base subobject in the most-derived object.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: OOPS Concepts, Programming in C++ and JAVA; source/basis: C++ working draft, virtual base classes and multiple inheritance: https://eel.is/c++draft/class.mi

questions.topic: OOPS Concepts, Programming in C++ and JAVA
questions.stem: Which statement about constructors in Java is correct?
options: Constructors are inherited by subclasses just like public instance methods
A subclass may inherit a superclass constructor and change only its return type
Constructors are not inherited; a subclass constructor invokes a superclass constructor explicitly or through an implicit `super()` when permitted
A constructor must be declared static to be inherited
explanations: Constructors are not inherited as methods.
A constructor has no return type to change and is not inherited.
Correct. A subclass constructor must initialise the superclass portion, using an explicit constructor invocation or an implicit no-argument super call when available.
Constructors cannot be declared static.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: OOPS Concepts, Programming in C++ and JAVA; source/basis: Java Language Specification, §8.8 constructors and §8.8.7 constructor bodies

questions.topic: OOPS Concepts, Programming in C++ and JAVA
questions.stem: Which statement about a C++ friend function is correct?
options: It is a member function automatically stored in the class's object layout
It is not a member of the class, but it may access the class's private and protected members when declared as a friend
It can access only public members
It must be virtual
explanations: A friend function is not made a class member merely by the friend declaration.
Correct. Friendship grants access rights but does not make the function a member.
The purpose of friendship is to permit specified non-members to access non-public members.
A non-member friend function cannot be virtual.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: OOPS Concepts, Programming in C++ and JAVA; source/basis: C++ working draft, friend declarations: https://eel.is/c++draft/class.friend

questions.topic: OOPS Concepts, Programming in C++ and JAVA
questions.stem: A Java class implements two unrelated interfaces that provide the same default instance method signature. What must the class normally do to resolve the conflict?
options: Override the method and provide an implementation or explicitly select a suitable interface default
Do nothing; the JVM randomly chooses one default method
Declare both interfaces as abstract classes
Delete one interface at runtime
explanations: Correct. The implementing class must resolve the inherited default-method conflict, commonly by overriding and optionally using `InterfaceName.super.method()`.
Java does not select conflicting defaults randomly.
Interfaces are not converted into abstract classes by this conflict.
Interfaces are part of the type declaration and cannot be deleted at runtime to resolve compilation.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: OOPS Concepts, Programming in C++ and JAVA; source/basis: Java Language Specification, §8.4.8 and §9.4.1, interface default methods

questions.subtopic: Gini impurity calculation for a binary decision-tree node
questions.stem: A decision-tree node contains 70% positive and 30% negative examples. Using Gini impurity G=1−Σpᵢ², what is the node's impurity?
explanations: 0.21 is the product of the two class proportions, not the stated Gini formula.
0.30 is the minority-class proportion, not the impurity.
0.70 is the majority-class proportion, not the impurity.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Data Mining; source/basis: Han, Kamber and Pei, Data Mining: Concepts and Techniques, decision-tree impurity measures

questions.stem: For a binary classifier, an ROC AUC of 0.90 is most accurately interpreted as:
options: The classifier is correct on exactly 90% of all records at every threshold
A randomly selected positive example is ranked above a randomly selected negative example with probability about 0.90
The false-positive rate is always 0.10
The classifier has exactly 90% precision
explanations: AUC is threshold-independent ranking performance, not accuracy at every threshold.
Correct. AUC has the probabilistic ranking interpretation for a randomly chosen positive-negative pair.
The false-positive rate varies with the selected threshold.
Precision depends on the threshold and class prevalence; it is not equal to AUC.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Data Mining; source/basis: Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, ROC analysis

questions.stem: A k-nearest-neighbours classifier uses Euclidean distance. One numeric feature ranges from 0 to 1, while another ranges from 0 to 100,000. What is the main risk if the features are used without scaling?
options: The large-range feature can dominate the distance calculation and distort neighbour selection
The small-range feature is automatically multiplied by 100,000
Euclidean distance becomes undefined
The algorithm changes into a decision tree
explanations: Correct. Differences on a large numeric scale can dominate the sum of squared coordinate differences.
No automatic rescaling occurs in ordinary Euclidean distance.
Euclidean distance remains mathematically defined for these finite numeric features.
Feature scaling does not change k-NN into another classifier.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Data Mining; source/basis: Han, Kamber and Pei, Data Mining: Concepts and Techniques, data preprocessing and k-NN

questions.stem: In agglomerative hierarchical clustering, how is the distance between two clusters defined by complete linkage?
options: The minimum pairwise distance between their points
The distance between their centroids only
The average of all within-cluster distances
The maximum pairwise distance between a point in one cluster and a point in the other
explanations: The minimum pairwise distance defines single linkage.
Centroid distance is a different cluster-distance definition.
Average linkage uses the average cross-cluster pairwise distance.
Correct. Complete linkage uses the maximum cross-cluster pairwise distance.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Data Mining; source/basis: Han, Kamber and Pei, Data Mining: Concepts and Techniques, hierarchical clustering

questions.stem: An association rule A→B has confidence 0.80, and B occurs in 0.40 of all transactions. Using conviction=(1−support(B))/(1−confidence(A→B)), what is its conviction?
explanations: 0.75 is not obtained from the stated numerator and denominator.
1.20 is not the ratio of 0.60 to 0.20.
2.00 would require a numerator of 0.40 with denominator 0.20.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Data Mining; source/basis: Han, Kamber and Pei, Data Mining: Concepts and Techniques, association-rule interestingness measures

questions.stem: Which representation is central to the Eclat frequent-itemset mining algorithm?
options: A vertical layout storing, for each item, the transaction-ID set in which it occurs
A horizontal table of candidate itemsets generated only by breadth-first enumeration
A decision tree whose leaves are class labels
A neural-network weight matrix
explanations: Correct. Eclat uses vertical transaction-ID lists (tidsets) and intersects them to calculate support of combined itemsets.
The horizontal candidate-generation description is closer to the classic Apriori approach.
A decision tree is a supervised classification model, not the Eclat representation.
A neural-network weight matrix is unrelated to frequent-itemset mining.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Data Mining; source/basis: Han, Kamber and Pei, Data Mining: Concepts and Techniques, Eclat algorithm

questions.stem: In a support vector machine with a hard-margin linear separator, which training points determine the position of the maximum-margin decision boundary?
options: All training points equally, regardless of their distance from the boundary
Only the support vectors lying closest to the separating hyperplane
Only points classified correctly far from the boundary
Only points from the majority class
explanations: Distant non-support points do not individually determine the maximum-margin boundary once the margin constraints are satisfied.
Correct. The support vectors are the constraint-active points closest to the hyperplane and determine the maximum-margin separator.
Points far from the boundary generally do not define the margin.
The support vectors can come from both classes; majority-class membership is not the rule.
questions.basis: Official Paper II syllabus: Data Mining; source/basis: Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning; standard support-vector-machine maximum-margin formulation
